Q: 2 scans instead of 1 in GROUP BY x HAVING EXISTS(..) A:

In that subquery, you can run as many filtered and unfiltered aggregates as you want, repeated or original, and the planner won't care one bit as long as it can determine they're valid in the outer query.

I'm not sure how the code you referenced is relevant. That's a special optimisation for min() and/or max() calls that has nothing to do with the case at hand. It says so right on the tin:

/*-------------------------------------------------------------------------
 *
 * planagg.c
 *    Special planning for aggregate queries.
 *
 * This module tries to replace MIN/MAX aggregate functions by subqueries
 * of the form
 *      (SELECT col FROM tab
 *       WHERE col IS NOT NULL AND existing-quals
 *       ORDER BY col ASC/DESC
 *       LIMIT 1)
...
*/

The fragment you pointed at belongs to can_minmax_aggs

/*
 * can_minmax_aggs
 *      Examine all the aggregates in the query, and check if they are
 *      all MIN/MAX aggregates.  If so, build a list of MinMaxAggInfo
 *      nodes for them.
 *
 * Returns false if a non-MIN/MAX aggregate is found, true otherwise.
 */
static bool
can_minmax_aggs(PlannerInfo *root, List **context)

and it's meant to give up in case someone does only call min() but also adds some fancy filter() conditions that complicate the optimisation techniques that the whole thing tries to apply.

FILTER emulation with a CASE expression does not get you a simpler plan in PostgreSQL. If anything, it obfuscates your intention to the planner.

the planner misses the optimization of computing both aggregates in a single pass

That whole test case is there to make sure it can compute them in a single pass, because otherwise that syntax isn't supported. If it can't push it up and out, it doesn't spawn an additional aggregated subquery - it just throws an error.

Q: window.open() parameters not working in Edge A:

We encountered the same issues. It turned out that if the "location=" parameter is included, Edge completely ignores all the parameters.

Removing that parameter allowed the others to work.

window.open (url, null,"height=200,width=200,status=yes,toolbar=yes,menubar=yes,location=yes,resizable=yes");

Fails - window opens with same size as parent window.

window.open (url, null,"height=200,width=200,status=yes,toolbar=yes,menubar=yes,resizable=yes");

Works fine - window opens 200x200 pixels.

Q: how to compare current date to a future date and validate it in javascript A: 

var d1 = new Date();
var d2 = new Date(d1);

console.log(d1 == d2); // prints false (wrong!) 
console.log(d1 === d2); // prints false (wrong!)
console.log(d1 != d2); // prints true  (wrong!)
console.log(d1 !== d2); // prints true  (wrong!)
console.log(d1.getTime() === d2.getTime()); // prints true (correct)

Also you can do <,>,>=,<= etc
